questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of reaching the k-th node of a singly linked list?

options.text: O(k) — you must follow k pointers from the head
O(1) — via address arithmetic like an array
O(log k) — the list is kept sorted

questions.explanation: Nodes are not contiguous, so there is no O(1) indexing; you traverse pointer by pointer, which costs O(k).

questions.prompt: Why is inserting a new node at the head of a linked list O(1)?

options.text: You create one node and repoint the head; nothing shifts
The list copies all elements into a bigger block
The head is stored in a hash table
Every element moves one position right

questions.explanation: Unlike an array, no elements move — you just allocate a node, point it at the old head, and update the head pointer.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing linked lists and arrays are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrays give O(1) indexing; linked lists do not
Linked lists give O(1) insertion at the head; arrays do not
Linked lists use extra memory per node for pointers
Linked lists allow O(1) random access by index

questions.explanation: Arrays win at indexing and memory density; linked lists win at O(1) head/known-node splicing. Linked lists have no O(1) random access.

questions.prompt: A placeholder node that always precedes the first real element, removing head/empty edge cases, is called a ______ node. (dummy or ______)
questions.explanation: A sentinel (a.k.a. dummy) node gives every real node a predecessor, so insertion/deletion at the head needs no special case.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to insert a new value at the head of a singly linked list.

items.text: Create a new node holding the value

questions.explanation: Build the node, point it at the current head, then move the head to the new node — order matters so you don't lose the old head.

questions.prompt: Match each linked-list operation with its time complexity.

pairs.left: Delete a node you hold (doubly linked)

questions.explanation: Head insertion and deleting a held node in a doubly linked list are constant; searching and indexing require traversal.
